newsitem.title: SWEDEN: Swedish Riksbank repeats no need to move repo.
newsitem.headline: Swedish Riksbank repeats no need to move repo.

text.p: Sweden's central bank governor Urban Backstrom repeated on Thursday that there was no need to move the Riksbank's key repurchase rate.

In a speech to the parliamentary finance committee, he also said that Statistics Sweden's new method of calculating the consumer price index (CPI) did not change the bank's view on underlying inflation.

"The central bank currently sees no need to change the repo rate," Backstrom said. "The recovery of the economy is supported by last year's repo rate cuts in combination with the development of the crown."
"Inflation seems to be under control according to information available today."
He said the outlook for the ongoing growth in the Swedish economy was more positive than for a long time following the slowing down of inflation in 1996.
The Riksbank cut the repo to 4.10 percent from 8.91 percent last year, but has not moved it in 1997.

"The repo rate has been kept unchanged at the beginning of 1997 but the crown has at the same time weakened by between four and five percent," Backstrom said. "The economy has thus been further stimulated.
"A great part of the result of the development of the rate and the crown probably still lies ahead of us because it takes time before the monetary policy achieves full effect," he said.
He said economic developments so far largely confirmed the picture given in the central bank's latest inflation report in March.
"Various forward-looking indicators show that the Swedish economy is again facing a period of increased production growth," Backstrom said.
"Simultaneously, we can most probably expect continuously low price rises this year and next year," he added.
Earlier on Thursday, Statistics Sweden said consumer prices rose by 0.5 percent in April from March for a year-on-year rise of 0.2 percent.

It revised the consumer price index (CPI) figures for 1996 and 1995, saying prices rose 0.8 percent in 1996 and 2.8 percent in 1995, year-on-year. Previously, the agency had said CPI rose 0.7 percent in 1996 and 2.9 percent in 1995.
The agency revised the figures to take into account costs for house owners when they change their mortgages to get more favourable interest rates.
"These changes however do not affect the central bank's analysis of underlying inflation," Backstrom said.
